subject: Mathematics
board: Pearson Edexcel (KS3 Maths Progress, building to Edexcel GCSE Mathematics 1MA1)
source: School scheme of work: Pearson KS3 Maths Progress (2nd ed.) Year 8 Autumn, Unit 1 Number and Unit 2 Area and volume (ks3_maths_a_p_sow3.xlsx), in the scheme's order; INSET lesson standard.

lessons.title: Written calculations with decimals
lessons.bigQuestion: Where does the decimal point go, and how can we be sure?
objectives: Add and subtract decimals using columns
Choose between mental and written methods
Check answers using estimation and inverse operations
successCriteria: Add and subtract decimals with the points lined up
Add more than two numbers with different numbers of decimal places
Explain errors in someone else's working
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: adding measured masses; Business: totals on a receipt
lessons.smsc: Moral: accuracy and honesty when handling money and measurements

keywords.def: a digit position after the decimal point
a zero used to keep digits in their correct place
an approximate answer from rounded numbers
the opposite operation used to check

starter: What is the value of the 4 in 2.648?

teach.heading: Line up the decimal points
bullets: Then add or subtract as usual
teach.note: Model and narrate each step.

teach.heading: Subtracting with place holders
bullets: Exchange across the point as normal
teach.note: Example: 12 − 4.37 = 7.63. Ask: 'Why must we write 12.00?'

teach.heading: Mental or written?
teach.note: Give three calculations and ask pupils to choose a method and justify it.

teach.heading: Estimate, then check
bullets: Use the inverse: subtract to check addition

teach.heading: Check: decimals
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: Work out 5.3 + 2.47
check.why: 5.30 + 2.47 = 7.77 with the points lined up. The other answers come from lining up digits instead of points, or subtracting.

independent: Extend: A recipe needs 0.75 kg flour, 0.3 kg sugar and 0.125 kg butter. Find the total mass, and how much flour is left from a 2 kg bag.
Stretch: Find the missing digits: 3.□7 + □.85 = 9.12
lessons.homework: Use a supermarket receipt (or the sample one) to add up the items with a written method and check against the total.
lessons.send: Support: place-value columns with the point printed. Stretch: missing-digit problems.

lessons.title: Multiplying and dividing decimals
lessons.bigQuestion: Does multiplying always make a number bigger?
objectives: Multiply decimals using a whole-number method
Divide a decimal by a whole number
Use estimation to place the decimal point
successCriteria: Multiply a decimal by a whole number
Multiply two decimals and place the point correctly
Explain why multiplying by 0.5 makes a number smaller
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: calculating with measurements; Business: unit prices
lessons.smsc: Social: fair sharing of costs between friends

keywords.def: separates whole numbers from parts of a whole
the result of a multiplication
the result of a division
an approximate answer to check against

starter: Round 6.48 to the nearest whole number

teach.heading: Multiply as whole numbers, then adjust
bullets: Count decimal places in the question
The answer has the same number
teach.note: Model and show the estimate as a check.

model.problem: Work out 3.4 × 2.6

teach.heading: Multiplying by numbers less than 1
teach.note: Answer the big question: multiplying by a number between 0 and 1 makes it smaller.

misconception.wrong: Multiplying always makes a number bigger

teach.heading: Dividing a decimal by a whole number
teach.note: Example: 17.4 ÷ 6 = 2.9. Then 7 ÷ 4 = 1.75 by writing 7.00.

model.problem: Work out 25.2 ÷ 4

teach.heading: Check: place the point
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.why: Two decimal places in the question, so 9.36. Estimate: 5 × 2 = 10 confirms it.

independent: Extend: Petrol costs £1.42 per litre. Find the cost of 38.5 litres to the nearest penny.
Stretch: Find two decimals whose product is 0.24 and whose sum is 1. Find another pair whose product is 1.2.
exit: Is 50 × 0.9 bigger or smaller than 50? Why?
lessons.homework: Calculate the cost of five items bought by weight (e.g. 1.4 kg of apples at £2.35 per kg), estimating first.
lessons.send: Support: grid method for decimal multiplication. Stretch: dividing by a decimal.

lessons.title: Divisibility rules
lessons.bigQuestion: How can you tell if 3 744 is divisible by 9 without dividing?
objectives: Know and use divisibility rules for 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 10
Use divisibility to find factors quickly
Explain why a divisibility rule works
successCriteria: Use the rules for 2, 3, 5 and 10
Use the rules for 4, 6, 8 and 9
Explain why the digit-sum rule works for 3 and 9
lessons.crossCurricular: Computing: checking codes such as ISBNs; History: number systems
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the order and patterns in numbers

keywords.def: can be divided exactly with no remainder
the total of a number's digits
a number that divides exactly into another
a reliable test that always works

teach.heading: The rules
teach.note: Go through the table and test each with 3 744.

teach.heading: Testing a big number
bullets: Write yes or no with a reason
teach.note: Model all the tests.

model.problem: Is 3 744 divisible by 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 9?
steps: By 2 and 3, so by 6: yes; 744 = 8 × 93: by 8, yes

teach.heading: Why the digit sum works
teach.note: Higher attainers love this. Show that the multiples of 9 vanish, leaving the digit sum. That is why it works for 3 and 9 only.

teach.heading: The rule for 6
teach.note: Ask: 'Does 'divisible by 3 and 4' mean divisible by 12?' Yes, because 3 and 4 share no factors. But '2 and 4' does not mean 8.

misconception.wrong: Divisible by 2 and 4, so divisible by 8 (e.g. 12)
misconception.right: Combine only when the numbers share no factor: 2 and 3 → 6

teach.heading: Check: divisibility
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: Which number is divisible by 9?
check.why: 4 + 5 + 1 + 8 = 18, which is divisible by 9. The other digit sums are 10, 10 and 16, none divisible by 9.

practice: Find a digit to make 47□ divisible by 6
independent: Core: Test 5 040 for divisibility by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 10
Extend: Find the smallest 4-digit number divisible by 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6.
Stretch: Find all digits d so that the number 52d6 is divisible by 4 and by 9. Explain why there may be none.
exit: Why is 135 divisible by 5 but not by 10?
lessons.homework: Write down any five 4-digit numbers (e.g. phone digits) and test each for divisibility by 3, 4, 6 and 9.
lessons.send: Support: rules card. Stretch: research the rule for 11.

lessons.title: Calculating with negative integers
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is a negative times a negative a positive?
objectives: Add and subtract negative numbers
Multiply and divide negative numbers
Use negatives with the priority of operations
successCriteria: Add and subtract with negatives
Multiply and divide with negatives using the sign rules
Explain the sign rules using patterns
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: temperature changes; Business: profit and loss
lessons.smsc: Moral: debt and its effects; why Islam forbids riba (رِبَا, interest) on loans

keywords.def: a whole number: positive, negative or zero
less than zero
+ or − in front of a number
the result of multiplying

teach.heading: A pattern explains the rule
bullets: Each step down, the answer falls by 3
Keep the pattern going past zero
teach.note: Build the table live. Ask pupils to continue it.

teach.heading: The sign rules
teach.note: Practise quick-fire: −6 × 4, −20 ÷ −5, 18 ÷ −3.

teach.heading: Negatives with BIDMAS
teach.note: This trips up calculator users. Show both on screen.

teach.heading: Check: sign rules
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.why: −24 ÷ −6 = 4, then 4 × −2 = −8. Left to right for ÷ and ×.

independent: Extend: A business makes a loss of £350 in each of 4 months, then a profit of £900 in each of 2 months. What is its overall result?
Stretch: Find two integers whose product is −36 and whose sum is 5. How many pairs have a product of −36?
lessons.homework: Make a negative-number multiplication grid from −5 to 5 and colour the positive and negative answers. Describe the pattern.
lessons.send: Support: sign-rule card and number line. Stretch: powers of negative numbers.

lessons.title: Powers and roots
lessons.bigQuestion: How quickly do numbers grow when we keep multiplying?
objectives: Calculate squares, cubes, square roots and cube roots
Know when a square root can be negative
Use a calculator for powers and roots
successCriteria: Recall squares to 15² and cubes of 1 to 5 and 10
Calculate with roots and powers on a calculator
Explain why √25 has two answers but ∛27 has only one real answer
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: area and volume units; Computing: powers of 2 in binary
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at fast growth, such as the story of rice on a chessboard

keywords.def: how many times a number is multiplied by itself
a number multiplied by itself three times
a number that squares to give the original
a number that cubes to give the original

teach.heading: Squares and cubes
teach.note: Show a cube made of smaller cubes. 3³ = 27 small cubes.

teach.heading: Roots
teach.note: The √ sign means the positive root. Ask: 'What is ∛(−8)?' (−2, since −2 × −2 × −2 = −8.)

teach.heading: Calculator skills
teach.note: Model on an online scientific calculator on screen.

model.problem: Work out 2⁵ + ∛343

teach.heading: Check: roots
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: Which number has two square roots, 6 and −6?
check.why: 6² = 36 and (−6)² = 36. −36 has no real square root; 216 = 6³.

independent: Extend: A cube has a volume of 512 cm³. Find the length of one edge and the area of one face.
Stretch: Find a number that is both a square and a cube between 1 and 1000 (other than 1). Find all of them. What do you notice?
lessons.homework: One grain of rice on square 1 of a chessboard, 2 on square 2, 4 on square 3… Write the number on squares 1 to 12 as powers of 2 and work them out.
lessons.send: Support: squares and cubes table on screen. Stretch: powers of 2 and binary.

lessons.title: Powers, roots and brackets
lessons.bigQuestion: How do calculators 'know' which part to do first?
objectives: Calculate combinations of powers, roots and brackets
Use the priority of operations accurately
Enter calculations correctly into a calculator
successCriteria: Work out calculations with a power and one other operation
Work out multi-step calculations with roots, powers and brackets
Enter fractions and roots correctly into a calculator, using brackets
lessons.crossCurricular: Computing: operator precedence in code; Science: formulae such as E = mc²
lessons.smsc: Social: shared rules let us communicate clearly

keywords.def: the small number showing the power
the order in which operations are done
Brackets, Indices, Division and Multiplication, Addition and Subtraction
the inverse of a power

teach.heading: Roots count as indices
bullets: √ and ∛ are done at the I stage
Work inside the root sign first, like a bracket
teach.note: √(9 + 16) means add first: √25 = 5. Compare with √9 + √16 = 7.

teach.heading: A multi-step calculation
bullets: Keep the rest of the calculation
teach.note: Model, writing each line.

model.problem: Work out 5 + (12 − 2³) × √36

teach.heading: Fractions on a calculator
bullets: The fraction line is a hidden bracket
teach.note: Show (20 + 4)/(2 × 3) = 4 but typing 20 + 4 ÷ 2 × 3 gives 26.

teach.heading: Check: order
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: Work out 3 × 2² + 1
check.why: Indices first: 2² = 4, then 3 × 4 = 12, then + 1 = 13. A works out (3 × 2)² + 1 = 37, ignoring the order of operations.

independent: Extend: Use a calculator: (a) (3.2² + 4.1) ÷ (2.5 − 0.9) (b) √(7.8² − 3.6²) to 2 decimal places
Stretch: Using 2, 3 and 4 once each with powers, roots and brackets, make the largest and smallest positive numbers you can.
exit: How would you type (15 + 9) ÷ (2 + 4) into a calculator?
lessons.homework: Write five calculations that use a power, a root and brackets with a final answer of 10.
lessons.send: Support: BIDMAS step frame. Stretch: nested brackets and powers of fractions.

lessons.title: Index notation and prime factor decomposition
lessons.bigQuestion: Is there only one way to build a number from primes?
objectives: Use index notation for repeated factors
Write a number as a product of its prime factors
Use a factor tree or repeated division
successCriteria: Draw a factor tree to find prime factors
Write the product in index form
Use the prime factors to tell if a number is a square or cube
lessons.crossCurricular: Computing: prime factors in internet security (RSA encryption)
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: every number has one unique 'fingerprint' of primes

keywords.def: a factor that is a prime number
writing a number as a product of prime factors
using powers to show repeated multiplication, e.g. 2³
a diagram splitting a number into factors until all are prime

teach.heading: Factor trees
teach.note: Show that 2 × 30 and 6 × 10 both give the same primes in the end. That answers the big question: the decomposition is unique.

model.problem: Write 120 as a product of prime factors

teach.heading: Repeated division
bullets: Divide by the smallest prime that works

teach.heading: Index form errors
bullets: Multiply out to check your answer
teach.note: Ask: 'What is wrong with 72 = 2 × 4 × 9?' (4 and 9 are not prime.)

teach.heading: Squares and cubes from primes
bullets: All indices even: a square number
All indices multiples of 3: a cube number
teach.note: 144 = 2⁴ × 3²: all even, so square; √144 = 2² × 3 = 12.

teach.heading: Check: product of primes
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: Which is 84 written as a product of prime factors?
check.why: 2 × 2 × 3 × 7 = 84 and all are prime. B and D contain 21 and 4, which are not prime.

practice: Write 36 as a product of prime factors in index form
Write 150 as a product of prime factors
independent: Core: Write in index form: (a) 60 (b) 98 (c) 200 (d) 252
Extend: 2ᵃ × 3ᵇ = 432. Find a and b.
Stretch: Use prime factors to find the smallest number you must multiply 90 by to get a square number, and the smallest to get a cube number.
exit: Write 48 as a product of primes in index form.
Is 2² × 3⁴ a square number? How do you know?
lessons.homework: Find the prime factor decomposition of your house number, your age multiplied by 10, and the current year.
lessons.send: Support: list of primes to 50 and partly drawn trees. Stretch: number of factors from the prime decomposition.

lessons.title: HCF and LCM using prime factors
lessons.bigQuestion: When will two buses that leave together next leave together again?
objectives: Find the HCF and LCM using prime factors
Use a Venn diagram to organise prime factors
Solve problems involving HCF and LCM
successCriteria: Find HCF and LCM of two numbers by listing
Use a Venn diagram of prime factors
Decide whether a problem needs the HCF or the LCM, and explain why
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: bus and train timetables; Design: tiling a floor
lessons.smsc: Social: planning fairly shared groups and events

keywords.def: the largest number that divides into both numbers
the smallest number that both numbers divide into
overlapping circles to show shared and unshared items
shared by both

starter: Write 60 as a product of primes

teach.heading: Prime factors in a Venn diagram
bullets: Shared primes go in the overlap
LCM: multiply everything in the diagram
teach.note: Model 60 = 2² × 3 × 5 and 72 = 2³ × 3². Overlap: 2, 2, 3.

model.problem: Find the HCF and LCM of 60 and 72

teach.heading: Which do I need?
bullets: Split into equal largest groups: HCF
teach.note: Sort five problems into HCF or LCM. Read them aloud.

left.title: HCF problems
points: Largest square tile for a floor
Cutting ribbons into equal longest lengths

right.title: LCM problems
points: Buying equal numbers of rolls and burgers

teach.heading: HCF and LCM mixed up
bullets: The HCF is never bigger than the smaller number
The LCM is never smaller than the larger number
teach.note: Use this as a sense check.

misconception.right: HCF must be ≤ 60; 360 is the LCM

teach.heading: Check: HCF or LCM
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: Bus A leaves every 12 minutes and bus B every 20 minutes. Both leave at 8:00. When do they next leave together?
check.why: LCM of 12 and 20 is 60 minutes, so 9:00. A uses the HCF (4); B adds them.

practice: Find the HCF and LCM of 18 and 24 using prime factors
Is 'largest group' an HCF or LCM question?
independent: Core: Find the HCF and LCM of (a) 36 and 48 (b) 40 and 56 (c) 126 and 84
Extend: A floor measures 360 cm by 270 cm. What is the largest square tile that fits exactly? How many tiles are needed?
Stretch: The HCF of two numbers is 6 and their LCM is 72. Find two possible pairs.
exit: Which is needed: 'largest equal bags of sweets'?
lessons.homework: Write three real-life problems (one HCF, one LCM, one either) with full solutions.
lessons.send: Support: Venn diagram template. Stretch: three numbers in a three-circle Venn.

lessons.title: Estimation and checking
lessons.bigQuestion: How can you tell an answer is wrong without working it out?
objectives: Round to 1 significant figure to estimate
Estimate calculations with several operations
Use estimates to check calculator answers
successCriteria: Round numbers to 1 significant figure
Estimate multi-step calculations including division
Say whether an estimate is an over- or under-estimate and why
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: checking experimental results; Geography: estimating populations
lessons.smsc: Moral: checking our own work honestly before handing it in

keywords.def: a digit that tells you about the size of the number; the first non-zero digit is the first
an approximate answer using rounded values
the symbol for 'approximately equal to'
an estimate bigger than the exact answer

teach.heading: Estimating a calculation
teach.note: Model with a fraction calculation.

teach.heading: Dividing by a decimal
teach.note: Many pupils halve when dividing by 0.5.

teach.heading: Check: estimate
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: Which is the best estimate of 31.6 × 0.48?
check.why: 30 × 0.5 = 15. A and C have the point in the wrong place; D multiplies by 2 instead of halving.

independent: Extend: A pupil's calculator says 47.3 × 0.92 = 435.16. Use an estimate to show this is wrong, and suggest what went wrong.
Stretch: Estimate (3.92 × 0.0517) ÷ 0.198. Is your estimate bigger or smaller than the exact value? Justify without a calculator.
lessons.homework: Estimate the total cost of a weekly shop of ten items, then compare with the exact total.
lessons.send: Support: highlight the first significant digit. Stretch: estimating with powers and roots.

lessons.title: Number problem solving and review
lessons.bigQuestion: Which number skill from this unit would you trust yourself with in a real-life emergency?
objectives: Choose and combine number skills to solve problems
Show working clearly
Identify and correct own misconceptions
successCriteria: Solve one-step number problems
Solve multi-step problems combining several skills
Explain a strategy and correct errors in worked solutions
lessons.crossCurricular: Business: budgeting; Science: data calculations
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: perseverance (sabr) on hard problems

keywords.def: a plan for solving a problem
a problem that needs several calculations
give reasons for your answer
think about what went well and what to improve

starter: Write 90 as a product of primes

teach.heading: A problem-solving routine
bullets: What do I know? What do I need?
teach.note: Display the routine; pupils use it for every problem today.

teach.heading: A multi-step problem
teach.note: Model and ask pupils to name the skill used at each step.

model.problem: Plates come in packs of 12, cups in packs of 18. A school wants the same number of each for a dinner and needs at least 100. Cost: plates £3.75 per pack, cups £4.20 per pack. Find the cheapest total.

teach.heading: Spot the error
bullets: Each worked answer has one mistake
teach.note: Show three: (−3)² = −9; 2.4 × 0.3 = 7.2; 72 = 2² × 18. Pupils fix them.

teach.heading: Check: choose the skill
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: 36 boys and 48 girls are put into the largest possible equal teams with no mixing. What size is each team?
check.why: HCF of 36 and 48 is 12. A is the LCM; D adds them.

practice: Find the cost of 2.5 kg of rice at £1.84 per kg
The temperature falls from 4 °C by 2.5 °C every hour for 4 hours. What is it now?
independent: Core: Five mixed questions: (a) 3.6 × 0.4 (b) −45 ÷ −9 (c) 2³ × 3² (d) HCF of 28 and 42 (e) estimate 812 ÷ 39
Extend: Two lighthouses flash every 15 s and 25 s. They flash together at 21:00:00. How many times do they flash together before 21:10:00?
Stretch: Write your own multi-step problem that needs at least three skills from this unit, with a full worked solution.
exit: Which skill would you use to find when two events happen together again?
Rate your confidence 1 to 3 for: decimals, negatives, primes.
lessons.homework: Complete the Unit 1 review sheet (10 questions) and highlight the two topics you found hardest.
lessons.send: Support: problem cards with skill hints. Stretch: open problems with multiple answers.

lessons.title: Area of a triangle
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is the area of a triangle exactly half of a rectangle?
objectives: Derive the formula for the area of a triangle
Use A = ½ × b × h with the perpendicular height
Find a missing length given the area
successCriteria: Find the area of a right-angled triangle
Find the area of any triangle using the perpendicular height
Find a missing base or height from the area
lessons.crossCurricular: Art: triangles in Islamic geometric design; DT: roof shapes
lessons.smsc: Cultural: triangular structures in architecture around the world

keywords.def: the amount of space inside a 2D shape, in square units
the side the shape stands on
the height measured at right angles to the base
a rule written with letters

starter: Area of a rectangle 6 cm by 4 cm?
What units is area measured in?
Name a triangle with a right angle

teach.heading: Half a rectangle
bullets: A diagonal cuts a rectangle into 2 equal triangles
teach.note: Animate cutting a rectangle along a diagonal. Then show a non-right triangle fits in a rectangle twice too (cut and move the pieces).

misconception.right: Use the perpendicular height, at 90° to the base

teach.heading: Using the formula
bullets: Height is perpendicular to the base
teach.note: Model with a triangle base 9 cm, perpendicular height 6 cm, slant side 7 cm.

model.problem: Base 9 cm, perpendicular height 6 cm, slant side 7 cm. Find the area.

teach.heading: Working backwards
bullets: Put the area into the formula

teach.heading: Check: which height?
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: A triangle has base 10 cm, sides 8 cm and 7 cm, and perpendicular height 5 cm. What is its area?
check.why: ½ × 10 × 5 = 25. A uses the 8 cm side; C forgets to halve; D uses 7 cm.

practice: Find the area: base 8 cm, height 5 cm
Find the area: base 7 m, height 3 m
Area 24 cm², base 8 cm. Find the height.
independent: Core: Find the area of triangles with (a) b = 14 cm, h = 9 cm (b) b = 6.5 m, h = 4 m (c) b = 11 mm, h = 7 mm
Extend: A triangular sail has a base of 3.2 m and a height of 5.5 m. Sailcloth costs £18 per m². Find the cost.
Stretch: Draw three different triangles on a grid that each have an area of 12 cm². Explain why there are infinitely many.
exit: Area 18 cm², height 4 cm. Find the base.
lessons.homework: Find and measure three triangles at home (e.g. sandwiches, signs) and calculate their areas.
lessons.send: Support: grid paper and labelled diagrams with the height highlighted. Stretch: triangles on coordinate grids.

lessons.title: Area of parallelograms and trapezia
lessons.bigQuestion: How can cutting and rearranging a shape help us find its area?
objectives: Derive and use the formula for the area of a parallelogram
Derive and use the formula for the area of a trapezium
Find areas of compound shapes
successCriteria: Find the area of a parallelogram
Find the area of a trapezium
Find areas of compound shapes using several formulae
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: estimating the area of a field; DT: designing a garden
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: patterns of tessellating shapes in mosque tilework

keywords.def: a quadrilateral with two pairs of parallel sides
a quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides
always the same distance apart; never meet
a shape made of simpler shapes

starter: Area of a triangle: base 10 cm, height 7 cm
Area of a rectangle 9 cm by 5 cm
How many pairs of parallel sides has a square?

teach.heading: Parallelogram = rectangle
bullets: Cut off a triangle and slide it across
teach.note: Animate the cut and slide. Ask: 'What stays the same?' (Base and perpendicular height.)

teach.heading: Trapezium formula
bullets: a and b are the parallel sides
h is the perpendicular distance between them
teach.note: Show two copies making a parallelogram of base (a + b).

model.problem: Trapezium: parallel sides 6 cm and 10 cm, height 4 cm. Find the area.

teach.heading: Compound shapes
bullets: Split into rectangles, triangles and trapezia
teach.note: An L-shaped room: split into two rectangles, or a big rectangle minus a small one. Both give the same answer.

teach.heading: Using the slant side
teach.note: Same error as with triangles.

teach.heading: Check: trapezium
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: A trapezium has parallel sides 5 m and 9 m and height 6 m. Its area is…
check.why: ½ × (5 + 9) × 6 = 7 × 6 = 42. B forgets the half; A multiplies all three.

practice: Trapezium: parallel sides 4 m and 8 m, height 5 m
Area of an L-shape made of a 10 × 4 and a 3 × 6 rectangle
independent: Core: Find the areas: (a) parallelogram b = 15 cm, h = 8 cm (b) trapezium a = 7 cm, b = 13 cm, h = 6 cm (c) trapezium a = 2.5 m, b = 4.5 m, h = 3 m
Extend: A garden is a trapezium with parallel sides 12 m and 18 m, 9 m apart. Turf costs £4.50 per m². Find the cost of turfing it.
Stretch: A trapezium has area 60 cm², height 6 cm and one parallel side of 8 cm. Find the other parallel side.
exit: Area of a parallelogram: base 9 cm, height 4 cm?
Area of a trapezium: 3 cm, 7 cm, height 2 cm?
lessons.homework: Sketch a plan of a room or garden using rectangles and trapezia and calculate its total area.
lessons.send: Support: formula card and shapes with heights highlighted. Stretch: reverse problems.

how much a container holds; 1 litre = 1000 cm³

Divide to find the missing length

keywords.def: compares the sizes of two or more quantities
a ratio that cannot be divided further by a common factor
the biggest number that divides into all the numbers
one share of a ratio

hook.text: Which ratio is the odd one out?
hook.a: 6 : 8 simplifies to 3 : 4; the others all simplify to 2 : 3.

teach.heading: What a ratio shows
bullets: Green is 3/8 of all the beads

teach.heading: Simplifying
bullets: Divide every part by the HCF
Stop when no common factor is left
teach.note: Model, then pupils simplify 20 : 35 (4 : 7).

model.problem: Simplify 24 : 36.

teach.heading: Units first
bullets: Write both parts in the same unit
teach.note: 1 m : 25 cm: change metres to centimetres.

teach.heading: Three parts and 1 : n
teach.note: For 1 : n, divide both parts by the first part. Useful for comparing recipes.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: Simplify 18 : 12.
check.why: HCF 6 gives 3 : 2, in the same order as the question. 2 : 3 reverses the order; 6 : 4 and 9 : 6 are not fully simplified.

practice.q: A bag has 6 green and 9 yellow beads. Write green : yellow in simplest form and the fraction that is green.

independent.a: 3/8 are Arabic. 3 parts = 24, 1 part = 8, total 8 × 8 = 64 books

exit.q: Simplify 36 : 48.
Simplify 1.5 m : 30 cm.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Show me on 3.

independent.q: Core: Plot A(−3, −2), B(1, −2), C(1, 3). Find D to make a rectangle and work out its area.
Extend: (−1, 1) and (3, 1) are two corners of a square, joined by one side. Give both possible pairs of other corners.
Stretch: (−4, 1) and (2, 1) are the base of an isosceles triangle. The third corner is (x, 6). Find x.
independent.a: It must be above the middle of the base: x = −1

exit.q: Which quadrant is (5, −7) in?
What are the coordinates 6 left and 2 down from the origin?
Big question: why do we agree to write x first?
exit.a: So everyone reads a point the same way; (2, 5) and (5, 2) are different places.

lessons.homework: On squared paper draw axes from −6 to 6 and plot a geometric pattern (no people or faces) with at least one point in each quadrant; list its coordinates.
lessons.send: Support: printed axes; colour the quadrants. EAL: 'across' and 'up/down' gestures. Stretch: reflect your pattern in the y-axis and list the new points.
resources: Pearson KS3 Maths Progress (Second Edition) Year 7 9.3 Coordinates and midpoints (the school's KS3 scheme)

keywords.def: the point exactly halfway between two points
a straight line with two end points
flat, going across
straight up and down
add and divide by how many

hook.text: A is (−2, 1) and B is (6, 5). Where is the point exactly halfway between them?
hook.a: (2, 3): halfway across is the mean of −2 and 6; halfway up is the mean of 1 and 5.

teach.heading: Halfway along a number line
teach.note: Count in from both ends together.

bullets: The step from A to M equals the step from M to B

model.problem: M(1, 4) is the midpoint of AB. A is (−3, 7). Find B.
steps: x step from A to M: −3 to 1 is +4

teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: Which line passes through (4, −2) and (4, 7)?
check.why: Both points have x = 4, so the vertical line x = 4. y = 4 is horizontal.

practice.q: Where do x = −2 and y = 4 cross?

independent.q: Core: Find the midpoints of (a) (0, 0) and (8, 6) (b) (−4, 2) and (2, 10) (c) (3, −5) and (−3, 5)
Extend: M(−1, 2) is the midpoint of PQ and P is (3, −4). Find Q.
independent.a: Steps from P to M: −4 and +6, so Q(−5, 8)

independent.q: Stretch: x = −2, x = 4, y = 1 and y = 6 make a rectangle. Find its area, perimeter and the midpoint of a diagonal.

exit.q: Find the midpoint of (−2, 7) and (4, −1).
Is y = −3 horizontal or vertical?
Big question: why is the midpoint the mean of the coordinates?
exit.a: The mean is the value exactly halfway between two numbers, across and up.

lessons.homework: Plot four points of your choice, one in each quadrant; find the midpoint of each pair of neighbours and check on the grid.
lessons.send: Support: number lines for each coordinate. EAL: 'midpoint', 'horizontal', 'vertical' with gestures. Stretch: find the point a third of the way along a segment.
resources: Pearson KS3 Maths Progress (Second Edition) Year 7 9.3 Coordinates and midpoints and 9.5 Straight-line graphs (the school's KS3 scheme)
